author.name: Homer
author.lead: Homer was an ancient Greek poet who is traditionally credited as the author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, two epic poems that are foundational works of ancient Greek literature. Homer was highly revered in ancient Greek society and is considered one of the most influential authors in history. The question of Homer's identity and existence—dubbed the "Homeric Question"—continues to be debated, and scholars generally regard the two poems as the works of separate authors. The Iliad centers on a quarrel between King Agamemnon and the warrior Achilles during the last year of the Trojan War. The Odyssey chronicles the ten-year journey of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, back to his home after the fall of Troy. The epics depict man's struggle, the Odyssey especially so, as Odysseus perseveres through the punishment of the gods.

primary.heading: Textual transmission
primary.text: The orally transmitted Homeric poems were put into written form at some point between the eighth and sixth centuries BC. Some scholars believe that they were dictated to a scribe by the poet and that the current versions of the Iliad and Odyssey were in origin orally dictated texts. Albert Lord noted that the Balkan bards that he was studying revised and expanded their songs in their process of dictating. Some scholars hypothesise that a similar process of revision and expansion occurred when the Homeric poems were first written down. Other scholars hold that, after the poems were created in the eighth century, they continued to be orally transmitted with considerable revision until they were written down in the sixth century. After textualisation, the poems were each divided into 24 rhapsodes, today referred to as books, and labelled by the letters of the Greek alphabet.

Iliad.title: Iliad
Iliad.lead: The Iliad is one of two major surviving ancient Greek epic poems attributed to Homer. It is one of the oldest extant works of literature still widely read by modern readers. Like the Odyssey, the poem is divided into 24 books and was written in dactylic hexameter. It contains 15,693 lines in its standard edition. The Iliad is often regarded as the first substantial piece of European literature and is central to the study of classical philology. Set towards the end of the Trojan War, a 10-year siege of the city of Troy by a coalition of Mycenaean Greek states, the poem depicts significant events in the war's final weeks. In particular, it traces the anger (μῆνις) of Achilles, a celebrated warrior, from a fierce quarrel between him and King Agamemnon, to the death of the Trojan prince Hector. The narrative moves between wide battleground scenes and more personal interactions.

summaries.heading: Exposition (Books 1–4)
summaries.text: The story begins with an invocation to the Muse. The events take place towards the end of the Trojan War, fought between the Trojans and the besieging Achaeans (Homer interchangeably refers to the Greeks as "Achaeans", "Argives" or "Danaans"). The Achaean forces consist of armies from many different Greek kingdoms, led by their respective kings or princes. Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, acts as commander for these united armies. After nine years of fighting, the Achaeans had sacked some towns allied with Troy, and captured two maidens, Chryseis and Briseis. Agamemnon, the leader, took Chryseis as his concubine; Achilles, the Achaeans' greatest warrior, took Briseis. Chryses, father of Chryseis and a priest of Apollo, offered Agamemnon a large ransom for the return of his daughter. Agamemnon refused, against the wishes of the other Achaeans, and insulted the priest.

summaries.heading: Duels of Greek and Trojan Heroes (Books 5–7)
summaries.text: In the fighting, Diomedes kills many Trojans, including Pandarus, and defeats Aeneas. Aphrodite rescues him before he can be killed, but Diomedes attacks her and wounds the goddess's wrist. Apollo faces Diomedes and warns him against warring with gods, which Diomedes ignores. Apollo sends Ares to defeat Diomedes. Many heroes and commanders join in, including Hector, and the gods supporting each side try to influence the battle. Emboldened by Athena, Diomedes wounds Ares and puts him out of action. Hector rallies the Trojans and prevents a rout. Diomedes and the Trojan Glaucus find common ground after a duel and exchange unequal gifts, sparked by Glaucus's story of Bellerophon. Hector enters the city, urging his mother Hecuba to perform prayers and sacrifices, inciting Paris to battle, and bidding his wife Andromache and son Astyanax farewell on the city walls.

summaries.heading: The Rout of the Greeks (Books 8–15)
summaries.text: The next morning, Zeus prohibits the gods from interfering, and fighting begins anew. The Trojans prevail and force the Achaeans back to their wall. Hera and Athena are forbidden to help. Night falls before the Trojans can assail the Achaean wall. They camp in the field to attack at first light, and their watchfires light the plain like stars. Meanwhile, the Achaeans are desperate. Agamemnon admits his error and sends an embassy composed of Odysseus, Ajax, and Phoenix to offer Briseis and extensive gifts to Achilles, if he will return to the fighting. Achilles and his companion Patroclus receive the embassy, yet Achilles angrily refuses the offer, considering the slight to his honour too great. He declares that he will only return to battle if the Trojans reach his ships and threaten them with fire. The embassy returns, unsuccessful.

summaries.heading: The Death of Patroclus (Books 16–18)
summaries.text: Patroclus cannot stand to watch any longer and goes to Achilles, weeping. He admonishes him for his stubbornness and then asks him to allow him to fight in his place, wearing Achilles's armor so that he will be mistaken for him. Achilles relents and lends Patroclus his armor but sends him off with a stern warning to come back once the Trojans have been pushed back and not to pursue them to the walls. Achilles says that after all has been made right, he and Patroclus will take Troy together. Patroclus leads the Myrmidons into battle and arrives as the Trojans set fire to the first ships. The Trojans are routed by the sudden onslaught, and Patroclus begins his assault by killing Zeus's son Sarpedon, a leading ally of the Trojans. Patroclus, ignoring Achilles's command, pursues and reaches the gates of Troy, where Apollo himself stops him.

summaries.heading: The Rage of Achilles (Books 19–24)
summaries.text: In the morning, Thetis brings Achilles his new set of armor, only to find him weeping over Patroclus's body. Achilles arms for battle and rallies the Achaean warriors. Agamemnon gives Achilles all the promised gifts, including Briseis, but Achilles is indifferent to them. The Achaeans take their meal, but Achilles refuses to eat. His horse, Xanthos, prophesies Achilles's death; Achilles is indifferent. Achilles goes into battle, with Automedon driving his chariot. Zeus lifts the ban on the gods' interference, and the gods freely help both sides. Achilles, burning with rage and grief, slays many Trojans. Achilles slaughters half the Trojans' number in the river, clogging the water with bodies. The river god, Scamander, confronts Achilles and commands him to stop killing Trojans, but Achilles refuses. They fight until Scamander is beaten back by Hephaestus's firestorm.

themes.heading: Religion
themes.text: Ancient Greek religion had no strict organisation, rather arising out of the diverse beliefs of the Greek people. Adkins and Pollard state that "The early Greeks personalized every aspect of their world, natural and cultural, and their experiences in it. The earth, the sea, the mountains, the rivers, custom-law (themis), and one's share in society and its goods were all seen in personal as well as naturalistic terms". They perceived the world and its changes as a result of divine intervention or presence. Often, they found these events to be mysterious and inexplicable. In the Iliad, the Olympian gods, goddesses, and minor deities fight among themselves as well as participating in human warfare, often by interfering with mortals to oppose other gods.

themes.heading: Fate
themes.text: Fate (κήρ, kēr, 'fated death') propels most of the events of the Iliad. Gods and men abide by it, unable to contest or change it. It is highlighted and referenced throughout the narrative in multiple methods, for example, Zeus sending omens to seers such as Calchas, or Thetis's prophecies of Achilles's imminent death. Men and their gods continually speak of heroic acceptance and cowardly avoidance of one's fate. Fate does not determine every action, incident, and occurrence, but it does determine the outcome of life. For example, Patroclus prophesies Hector's death: Here, Patroclus alludes to his fated death by Hector's hand and to Hector's fated death by Achilles's hand. Each accepts the outcome of his life, yet persist regardless. However, fate is not always accepted outright. The first instance of this doubt occurs in Book 16.

themes.heading: Kleos
themes.text: Kleos (κλέος, "glory, fame") is the concept of glory earned in heroic battle. It is a fluctuating quality that can be given or taken, increased or decreased. In particular, Achilles is deeply concerned about his kleos. In Book 9 (9.410–16), Achilles poignantly tells Agamemnon's envoys – Odysseus, Phoenix, and Ajax – begging his reinstatement to battle about having to choose between two fates (διχθαδίας κήρας, 9.411). The passage reads: In forgoing his nostos, he will earn the greater reward of kleos aphthiton (κλέος ἄφθιτον, "fame imperishable"). In the poem, aphthiton (ἄφθιτον, "imperishable") occurs five other times, each occurrence denotes an object: Agamemnon's sceptre, the wheel of Hebe's chariot, the house of Poseidon, the throne of Zeus, and the house of Hephaestus.

themes.heading: Nostos
themes.text: Nostos (νόστος, "homecoming") occurs seven times in the poem, making it a minor theme in the Iliad itself. Yet the concept of homecoming is explored extensively in other Ancient Greek literature, especially in the postwar homeward fortunes experienced by the Atreidae (Agamemnon and Menelaus) and Odysseus (see the Odyssey).

themes.heading: Pride
themes.text: Pride drives the plot of the Iliad. The Achaeans gather on the plain of Troy to wrest Helen from the Trojans. Though the majority of the Trojans would gladly return Helen to the Achaeans, they defer to the pride of their prince, Alexandros, also known as Paris. Within this frame, Homer's work begins. At the start of the Iliad, Agamemnon's pride sets forth a chain of events that leads him to take from Achilles, Briseis, the girl he had originally given Achilles in return for his martial prowess. Due to this slight, Achilles refuses to fight and asks his mother, Thetis, to make sure that Zeus causes the Achaeans to suffer on the battlefield until Agamemnon comes to realize the harm he has done to him. Achilles's pride allows him to beg Thetis for the deaths of his Achaean friends.

themes.heading: Heroism
themes.text: The Iliad portrays the theme of heroism in a variety of different ways through different characters, mainly Achilles, Hector, Patroclus, etc. Though the traditional concept of heroism is often tied directly to the protagonist, who is meant to be written in a heroic light, the Iliad plays with this idea of heroism and does not make it explicitly clear who the true hero of the story is. The story of the Iliad follows the great Greek warrior Achilles, as well as his rage and the destruction it causes. Parallel to this, the story also follows the Trojan warrior Hector and his efforts to fight to protect his family and his people. It is generally assumed that, because he is the protagonist, Achilles is the hero of this story.

themes.heading: Timē
themes.text: Akin to kleos is timē (τιμή, "respect, honor"), the concept denoting the respectability an honorable man accrues with accomplishment (cultural, political, martial), per his station in life. In Book I, the Achaean troubles begin with King Agamemnon's dishonorable, unkingly behavior – first, by threatening the priest Chryses (1.11), then, by aggravating them in disrespecting Achilles, by confiscating Briseis from him (1.171). The warrior's consequent rancor against the dishonorable king ruins the Achaean military cause.

themes.heading: Hubris
themes.text: Hybris (Ὕβρις) plays a part similar to timē. The epic takes as its thesis the anger of Achilles and the destruction it brings. Anger disturbs the distance between human beings and the gods. Uncontrolled anger destroys orderly social relationships and upsets the balance of correct actions necessary to keep the gods away from human beings. Despite the epic's focus on Achilles's rage, hybris also plays a prominent role, serving as both kindling and fuel for many destructive events. Agamemnon refuses to ransom Chryseis out of hybris and harms Achilles's pride when he demands Briseis. Hubris forces Paris to fight against Menelaus. Agamemnon spurs the Achaeans to fight by calling into question Odysseus, Diomedes, and Nestor's pride, asking why they are cowering and waiting for help when they should be the ones leading the charge.

themes.heading: Mēnis
themes.text: The poem's initial word, μῆνιν (mēnin; acc. μῆνις, mēnis, "wrath", "rage", "fury"), establishes the Iliad's principal theme: the "Wrath of Achilles". His personal rage and wounded soldier's pride propel the story: the Achaeans' faltering in battle, the slayings of Patroclus and Hector, and the fall of Troy. In Book I, the Wrath of Achilles first emerges in the Achilles-convoked meeting between the Greek kings and the seer Calchas. King Agamemnon dishonours Chryses, the Trojan priest of Apollo, by refusing with a threat the restitution of his daughter, Chryseis – despite the proffered ransom of "gifts beyond count". The insulted priest prays to Apollo for help, and a nine-day rain of divine plague arrows falls upon the Achaeans. Moreover, in that meeting, Achilles accuses Agamemnon of being "greediest for gain of all men".

themes.heading: War
themes.text: Much of the Iliad focuses on death-dealing. To gain status, heroes must be good at killing. Though not as prevalent, there are instances where the author showcases the peaceful aspects of war. The first instance of this is in book 3 when Menelaus and Paris agree to fight a one-on-one to end the war. This conversation between Menelaus and Paris highlights the overwhelming desire for peace on both sides. Also in book 3, we see peace when the elders talk to Priam saying that though Helen is a beautiful woman, war is still too high a price to pay for one person. These events display the humanity of the war. In book 6, when Hector goes back into the city to visit his family, this event is another powerful show of peace because we get to see that Hector is more than a great warrior. He is a loving father and devoted husband.

themes.heading: Modern reconstructions of armour, weapons, and styles
themes.text: Few modern (archeologically, historically, and Homerically accurate) reconstructions of arms, armor, and motifs as described by Homer exist. Some historical reconstructions have been done by Salimbeti et al.

history.heading: Influence on classical Greek warfare
history.text: While the Homeric poems (particularly, the Iliad) were not necessarily revered scripture of the ancient Greeks, they were most certainly seen as guides that were important to the intellectual understanding of any educated Greek citizen. This is evidenced by the fact that in the late 5th century BC, "it was the sign of a man of standing to be able to recite the Iliad and Odyssey by heart." Moreover, it can be argued that the warfare shown in the Iliad, and the way it is depicted, had a profound and very traceable effect on Greek warfare in general. In particular, the effect of epic literature can be broken down into three categories: tactics, ideology, and the mindset of commanders. In order to discern these effects, it is necessary to take a look at a few examples from each of these categories.

primary.heading: Date and textual history
primary.text: The poem dates to the archaic period of Classical antiquity. Scholarly consensus mostly places it in the late 8th century BC, although some favour a 7th-century date. In any case, the terminus ante quem for the dating of the Iliad is 630 BC, as evidenced by reflection in art and literature. Herodotus, having consulted the Oracle at Dodona, placed Homer and Hesiod at approximately 400 years before his own time, which would place them at c. 850 BC. The historical backdrop of the poem is the time of the Late Bronze Age collapse, in the early 12th century BC. Homer is thus separated from his subject matter by about 400 years, the period known as the Greek Dark Ages. Intense scholarly debate has surrounded the question of which portions of the poem preserve genuine traditions from the Mycenaean period.

primary.heading: As oral tradition
primary.text: In antiquity, the Greeks applied the Iliad and the Odyssey as the bases of pedagogy. Literature was central to the educational-cultural function of the itinerant rhapsode, who composed consistent epic poems from memory and improvisation and disseminated them, via song and chant, in his travels and at the Panathenaic Festival of athletics, music, poetics, and sacrifice, celebrating Athena's birthday. Originally, Classical scholars treated the Iliad and the Odyssey as written poetry, and Homer as a writer, yet by the 1920s, Milman Parry (1902–1935) had launched a movement claiming otherwise. His investigation of the oral Homeric style – "stock epithets" and "reiteration" (words, phrases, stanzas) – established that these formulae were artifacts of oral tradition easily applied to a hexametric line.

primary.heading: Manuscripts
primary.text: There are more than 2000 manuscripts of Homer. Some notable manuscripts include: Rom. Bibl. Nat. gr. 6 + Matriti. Bibl. Nat. 4626 from 870 to 890 Venetus A = Venetus Marc, 822 from the 10th century Venetus B = Venetus Marc, 821 from the 11th century Ambrosian Iliad Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 20 Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 21 Codex Nitriensis (palimpsest) El Bahnasa area of Minya – Discovery of papyrus with text containing lines from Book Two of Homer's Iliad.

secondary.heading: English translations
secondary.text: George Chapman published his translation of the Iliad, in installments beginning in 1598, published in "fourteeners", a long-line ballad metre that "has room for all of Homer's figures of speech and plenty of new ones, as well as explanations in parentheses. At its best, as in Achilles's rejection of the embassy in Iliad Nine; it has great rhetorical power." It quickly established itself as a classic in English poetry. In the preface to his own translation, Pope praises "the daring fiery spirit" of Chapman's rendering, which is "something like what one might imagine Homer, himself, would have writ before he arrived at years of discretion". John Keats praised Chapman in the sonnet On First Looking into Chapman's Homer (1816).

tertiary.heading: Influence on arts and culture
tertiary.text: The Iliad, in addition to the Odyssey, became foundational school texts in classical Athens. Both texts were, by the end of the fifth century BC, widely known in the ancient Greek world. According to classicist Gregory Nagy, "Homer's Iliad, along with its companion-piece, the Odyssey, was venerated by the ancient Greeks themselves as the cornerstone of their civilization". According to literary scholar James Boyd White, "the Iliad at once defines a culture and subjects it to a set of fundamental criticisms". The Iliad was a popular work in classical Greece and remained so throughout the Hellenistic, Roman, and Byzantine periods. It is generally believed by most scholars to have "existed in some form by the mid-seventh century B.C.", although no explicit references to the Iliad from 650 to 550 BC survive and most references were in the form of literary allusions.

tertiary.heading: English
tertiary.text: William Shakespeare used the plot of the Iliad as source material for his play Troilus and Cressida but focused on a medieval legend, the love story of Troilus, son of King Priam of Troy, and Cressida, daughter of the Trojan soothsayer Calchas. The play, often considered to be a comedy, reverses traditional views on events of the Trojan War and depicts Achilles as a coward, Ajax as a dull, unthinking mercenary, etc. William Theed the elder made a bronze statue of Thetis as she brings Achilles his new armor forged by Hephaestus. It has been on display in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City since 2013. Robert Browning's poem Development discusses his childhood introduction to the matter of the Iliad and his delight in the epic, as well as contemporary debates about its authorship.

tertiary.heading: 20th-century arts
tertiary.text: Lesya Ukrainka wrote the dramatic poem "Cassandra" in 1901–1907 based on the Iliad. It describes the story of Cassandra, a prophetess. The fall of Troy (1911), an Italian silent film by Giovanni Pastrone, the first known movie adaptation of Homer's epic poem. "Achilles in the Trench" is one of the best-known of the war poems of the First World War and was written by Patrick Shaw-Stewart while waiting to be sent to fight at Gallipoli. The Private Life of Helen of Troy (1925), a book written by John Erskine which centres on Helen's afterlife in Sparta at the time Hermione is approaching marriage. Its dialogue is ironic and Helen is characterised as clever conversationalist able to self-analyse. The Private Life of Helen of Troy (1927), a silent comedy film directed by Alexander Korda.

tertiary.heading: Contemporary popular culture
tertiary.text: Eric Shanower's Image Comics series Age of Bronze, which began in 1998, retells the legend of the Trojan War. Dan Simmons's epic science fiction adaptation/tribute Ilium was released in 2003, receiving a Locus Award for best science fiction novel of 2003. Helen of Troy (2003), a TV miniseries told from the perspective of Menelaus which focuses on how Helen affected others around her, leaving the larger Trojan War as a background event. Troy (2004), a loose film adaptation of the Iliad, received mixed reviews, only grossing $133 million in the United States on a $185 million budget. Internationally, it was a commercial success, grossing $497 million worldwide. The Rage of Achilles (2009), by American author and Yale Writers' Conference founder Terence Hawkins, recounts the Iliad as a novel in modern, sometimes graphic language.

tertiary.heading: Sciences
tertiary.text: Psychiatrist Jonathan Shay wrote two books, Achilles in Vietnam: Combat Trauma and the Undoing of Character (1994) and Odysseus in America: Combat Trauma and the Trials of Homecoming (2002), which relate the Iliad and the Odyssey to posttraumatic stress disorder and moral injury as seen in the rehabilitation histories of combat veteran patients.

Q102561.label: Sisyphus
Q102561.description: king of Ephyra in Greek mythology
Q102561.lead: In Greek mythology, Sisyphus or Sisyphos is the founder and king of Ephyra (now known as Corinth). He reveals Zeus's abduction of Aegina to the river god Asopus, thereby incurring Zeus's wrath.

Q103107.label: Leto
Q103107.description: Greek mythological figure and mother of Apollo and Artemis
Q103107.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Leto is the mother of Apollo and Artemis. She is the daughter of the Titans Coeus and Phoebe, and the sister of Asteria.

Q1045730.label: Thersites
Q1045730.description: son of Agrius, Achean warrior in the Trojan War
Q1045730.lead: In Greek mythology, Thersites was a soldier of the Greek army during the Trojan War.

Q1057384.label: Pandarus
Q1057384.lead: Pandarus or Pandar, son of Lycaon, is a skilled Lycian archer who lived in the Troad city of Zeleia. In the Iliad, he is allied with Troy and appears in stories about the Trojan War.

Q1061747.label: Phoenix
Q1061747.description: Greek mythological character, son of Amyntor and tutor of Achilles
Q1061747.lead: In Greek mythology, Phoenix was the son of king Amyntor.

Q1061782.label: Rhesus of Thrace
Q1061782.lead: Rhesus is a mythical king of Thrace in The Iliad who fought on the side of Trojans. Rhesus arrived late to the battle and, while he slept in his camp after arriving, Diomedes and Odysseus killed him and stole his team of horses during a night raid.

Q1062299.label: Sthenelus
Q1062299.lead: In Greek mythology, Sthenelus was a king of Tiryns and Mycenae, and the son of Perseus who founded the latter city.

Q1069769.label: Eetion
Q1069769.description: king of Thebe and father of Andromache
Q1069769.lead: In Greek mythology, Eëtion or Eetion is the king of the Anatolian city of Cilician Thebe. He is said to be the father of Andromache, the wife of the Trojan prince Hector.

Q1071946.label: Podalirius
Q1071946.lead: In Greek mythology, Podalirius or Podaleirius or Podaleirios was a son of Asclepius.

Q1077936.label: Gorgythion
Q1077936.lead: In Greek mythology, Gorgythion was one of the sons of King Priam of Troy at the time of the Trojan War and appears as a minor character in Homer's Iliad. His mother was Castianeira of Aisyme.

Q1081453.label: Glaucus
Q1081453.lead: In Greek mythology, Glaucus was a captain in the Lycian army under the command of his close friend and cousin Sarpedon. The Lycians in the Trojan War were allies of Troy.

Q108419.label: Rhea
Q108419.description: female Titan in Greek mythology, mother of Zeus and mother of Hera
Q108419.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhea, Rhia or Rheia was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She was the sister and wife of Cronus, and by him was the mother of Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Zeus.

Q109220.label: Boreas
Q109220.description: Greek mythological personification and god of the North wind, storms,, winter, loneliness, solitude, absence, lack, sadness, depression, calmness and serenity
Q109220.lead: Boreas is the Greek god of the cold north wind, storms, and winter. Although he was normally taken as the north wind, the Roman writers Aulus Gellius and Pliny the Elder both took Boreas as a northeast wind, equivalent to the Roman god Aquilo or Septentrio.

Q1108130.label: Charis
Q1108130.lead: Charis, is a goddess in Greek mythology. She is a member of the Charites (Ancient Greek: Χάριτες) — or Gratiae (Graces) in Roman mythology — who are goddesses of charm, beauty, nature, creativity and fertility.

Q112.label: Mars
Q112.description: Roman god of war, guardian of agriculture
Q112.lead: In ancient Roman religion and mythology, Mars is the god of war and also an agricultural guardian, a combination characteristic of early Rome. He is the son of Jupiter and Juno, and was pre-eminent among the Roman army's military gods.

Q11294144.label: Castor
Q11294144.description: Greek mythical figure, brother of Pollux

Q1134694.label: Scamander
Q1134694.lead: Scamander, also Skamandros or Xanthos (Ξάνθος), was a river god in Greek mythology.

Q1150.label: Mercury
Q1150.description: Roman god of trade, merchants, thieves and travel
Q1150.lead: Mercury is a major god in Roman religion and mythology, being one of the 12 Dii Consentes within the ancient Roman pantheon. He is the god of boundaries, commerce, communication (including divination), eloquence, financial gain, languages, luck, thieves, travelers, and trickery; he is also the guide of souls to the underworld.

Q1154473.label: Theano
Q1154473.description: priestess of Athena in Troy in Greek mythology
Q1154473.lead: In Greek mythology, Theano was the wife of Antenor and a priestess of Athena at Troy during the Trojan War.

Q1172040.label: Amyntor
Q1172040.description: son of Ormenos and father of Phoenix
Q1172040.lead: In Greek mythology, Amyntor was the son of Ormenus, and a king of Eleon or Ormenium. Amyntor's son Phoenix, on his mother's urgings, had sex with his father's concubine, Clytia or Phthia.

Q1173681.label: Coön
Q1173681.description: son of Antenor in Greek mythology
Q1173681.lead: In Greek mythology, Coön, also known as Cynon (Κύνων), was the eldest son of Antenor and Theano.

Q1178583.label: Laodice
Q1178583.lead: In Greek mythology, Laodice was the daughter of Priam of Troy and Hecuba. She was described as the most beautiful of Priam's daughters.

Q119919.label: Panthous
Q119919.description: priest of Apollo at Troy, son of Othrys
Q119919.lead: In Greek mythology, Panthous, son of Othrys, was an elder of Troy, husband of the "queenly" Phrontis and father of Euphorbus, Polydamas and Hyperenor. Alternatively, his wife was sometimes said to be Pronome, a daughter of Clytius, Priam's brother.

Q1199200.label: Pyraechmes
Q1199200.lead: In Greek mythology, Pyraechmes was, along with Asteropaeus, a leader of the Paeonians in the Trojan War.

Q12046224.label: Pollux
Q12046224.description: Greek mythical figure, brother of Castor

Q1205276.label: Polydamas
Q1205276.description: Trojan hero, son of Panthoos in the Iliad
Q1205276.lead: In Greek mythology, Polydamas was a lieutenant and friend of Hector during the Trojan War.

Q1206546.label: Laothoe
Q1206546.description: daughter of Altes in Greek mythology

Q122248.label: Heracles
Q122248.description: divine hero in Greek mythology, son of Zeus and Alcmene
Q122248.lead: Heracles, born Alcaeus (Ἀλκαῖος) or Alcides (Ἀλκείδης) was the greatest of the Greek heroes. He was considered the son of Zeus and Alcmene, and the foster son of Amphitryon.

Q122827552.label: Antimachus
Q122827552.description: mythological Greek character, advisor to Priam

Q1235379.label: Pasithea
Q1235379.description: one of the Charities in Greek mythology
Q1235379.lead: In Greek mythology, Pasithea, Pasithee or Pasitheia was one of the Charites and the wife of Hypnos. In the Dionysiaca, the epic poem of Nonnus (fifth century CE), she and the other Charites are the attendants of Aphrodite.

Q1241338.label: Thaleia
Q1241338.lead: In Greek mythology, Thalia or Thaleia was one of the fifty Nereids, marine-nymph daughters of the 'Old Man of the Sea' Nereus and the Oceanid Doris. Her name was derived from θάλλειν thállein which means "to flourish, to be green".

Q125046.label: Juno
Q125046.lead: Juno is a goddess in the ancient Roman religion, the protector and special counsellor of the state. She equates to Hera, queen of the gods in Greek mythology and a goddess of marriage.

Q125157191.label: Hippasus
Q125157191.description: Greek mythical character, father of Charops and Socus

Q126916.label: Minerva
Q126916.description: Roman goddess of wisdom and sponsor of arts, trade, and defense
Q126916.lead: Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom, justice, law, victory, and the sponsor of arts, trade, and strategy. She is also a goddess of warfare, though with a focus on strategic warfare, rather than the violence of gods such as Mars.

Q128176.label: Agamemnon
Q128176.description: son of Atreus in Greek mythology
Q128176.lead: In Greek mythology, Agamemnon was a king of Mycenae who commanded the Achaeans during the Trojan War. He was the son (or grandson) of King Atreus and Queen Aerope, the brother of Menelaus, the husband of Clytemnestra, and the father of Iphigenia, Iphianassa, Electra, Laodike, Orestes and Chrysothemis.

Q12878261.label: Itymoneus
Q12878261.description: character from Greek mythology, son of Hypeirochus

Q12958119.label: Latona
Q12958119.description: mother of Apollo and Diana in Roman mythology

Q130818.label: Atlas
Q130818.lead: In Greek mythology, Atlas is a Titan condemned to hold up the heavens or sky for eternity after the Titanomachy. Atlas also plays a role in the myths of two of the greatest Greek heroes: Heracles (Hercules in Roman mythology) and Perseus.

Q130832.label: Perseus
Q130832.description: legendary Greek hero and founder of Mycenae, demigod son of Zeus and Danae; famous for beheading the Gorgon Medusa
Q130832.lead: In Greek mythology, Perseus is the legendary founder of the Perseid dynasty. He was, alongside Cadmus and Bellerophon, the greatest Greek hero and slayer of monsters before the days of Heracles.

Q131090.label: Chaos
Q131090.lead: In the context of religious cosmogony, Chaos refers to the division of reality outside or in contrast to the ordered cosmos. As such it refers to a state, place, or time beyond the known, familiar, and reliable world, often said to be inhabited by strange, ominous, or demonic beings.

Q131125.label: Hebe
Q131125.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Hebe is the goddess of youth or of the prime of life. She was the cup-bearer for the gods of Mount Olympus, serving their nectar and ambrosia.

Q131157.label: Clytemnestra
Q131157.description: daughter of Tyndareus in Greek mythology
Q131157.lead: In Greek mythology, Clytemnestra is the wife of Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, and the half-sister of Helen of Troy. With Agamemnon, she is the mother of Iphigenia, Orestes, Electra, and Chrysothemis.

Q131588.label: Ganymede
Q131588.description: son of Tros in Greek mythology
Q131588.lead: In Greek mythology, Ganymede ( GAN-im-eed) or Ganymedes is a divine hero whose homeland was Troy. Homer describes Ganymede as the most handsome of mortals and tells the story of how he was abducted by the gods to serve as Zeus's cup-bearer in Olympus.

Q132543.label: Diana
Q132543.description: goddess of the hunt, the moon and birthing, equated with the Greek goddess Artemis
Q132543.lead: Diana is a goddess in Roman religion, primarily considered a patroness of the countryside and nature, hunters, wildlife, childbirth, crossroads, the night, and the Moon. She is equated with the Greek goddess Artemis, and absorbed much of Artemis' mythology early in Roman history, including a birth on the island of Delos to parents Jupiter and Latona, and a twin brother, Apollo, though she had an independent origin in Italy.

Q1328257.label: Elephenor
Q1328257.lead: In Greek mythology, Elephenor was the king of the Abantes of Euboea.

Q1330702.label: Archelochus
Q1330702.description: mythical Greek character, son of Antenor
Q1330702.lead: In Greek mythology, Archelochus was a son of Antenor and Theano. Along with his brother, Acamas, and Aeneas, he shared the command of the Dardanians fighting on the side of the Trojans.

Q1331212.label: Lycaon
Q1331212.description: figure in Greek mythology, son of Priam and Laothoe
Q1331212.lead: In Greek mythology, as recorded in Homer's Iliad, Lycaon was a son of Priam and Laothoe, daughter of the Lelegian king Altes.

Q1331224.label: Eudoros
Q1331224.description: Greek mythical character, leader of the Myrmidons
Q1331224.lead: In Greek mythology, Eudoros was the second of Achilles' five commanders at the Trojan War.

Q1343776.label: Crethon
Q1343776.lead: In Greek mythology, Crethon was an Achaean warrior, from Pharae in Messenia, who participated in the Trojan War.

Q134388.label: Saturn
Q134388.lead: Saturn was a god in ancient Roman religion, and a character in Roman mythology. He was described as a god of time, generation, dissolution, abundance, wealth, agriculture, periodic renewal and liberation.

Q1367860.label: Talthybius
Q1367860.lead: Talthybius was herald and friend to Agamemnon in the Trojan War. Talthybius is a Greek soldier who serves as both a messenger and a herald during the time of the Trojan War.

Q1367871.label: Thoas
Q1367871.lead: In Greek mythology, Thoas, a king of Aetolia, was the son of Andraemon and Gorge, and one of the heroes who fought for the Greeks in the Trojan War. Thoas had a son Haemon, and an unnamed daughter.

Q1378407.label: Euryalus
Q1378407.description: son of Mecisteus in Greek Mythology

Q1389473.label: Agelaos
Q1389473.description: Greek mythological character, Achaian killed by Hektor

Q140001.label: Eris
Q140001.lead: In Greek mythology, Eris is the goddess and personification of strife and discord, particularly in war, and in the Iliad (where she is the "sister" of Ares the god of war). According to Hesiod she was the daughter of primordial Nyx (Night), and the mother of a long list of undesirable personified abstractions, such as Ponos (Toil), Limos (Famine), Algea (Pains) and Ate (Delusion).

Q1446575.label: Orsilochus
Q1446575.description: son of Alpheus in Greek mythology

Q1495743.label: Ilus
Q1495743.description: son of Tros in Greek mythology, mythological founder of Troy
Q1495743.lead: In Greek mythology, Ilus was the founder of the city called Ilios or Ilion (Latinized as Ilium) to which he gave his name. When the latter became the chief city of the Trojan people it was also often called Troy, the name by which it is best known today.

Q15262316.label: Lycomedes
Q15262316.description: son of Creon in Greek mythology
Q15262316.lead: In Greek mythology, Lycomedes was a Theban armed sentry with Thrasymedes, son of Nestor during the Trojan War.

Q15711584.label: Cymodoce
Q15711584.lead: In Greek mythology, Cymodoce is one of the 50 Nereids, sea-nymph daughters of the 'Old Man of the Sea' Nereus and the Oceanid Doris. She is briefly mentioned in Statius' Silvae.

Q15736237.label: Hippodamas
Q15736237.description: Greek mythical character, son of Priam

Q15819831.label: Iasus
Q15819831.description: mythological Greek character, son of Sphelus

Q1588440.label: Eurypylus
Q1588440.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurypylus was a Thessalian king.

Q159168.label: Themis
Q159168.description: in ancient Greek mythology, a titaness, the personification of divine order, fairness, law, natural law, and custom, whose symbols are the scales of justice
Q159168.lead: In Greek mythology and religion, Themis is the goddess and personification of justice, divine order, law, and custom. She is one of the twelve Titan children of Gaia and Uranus, and the second wife of Zeus.

Q159666.label: Hector
Q159666.description: prince of Troy in Greek mythology
Q159666.lead: In Greek mythology, Hector was a Trojan prince, a hero, and the greatest warrior for Troy during the Trojan War. He is a major character in Homer's Iliad, where he leads the Trojans and their allies in the defense of Troy, killing countless Greek warriors.

Q1601938.label: Laodamia
Q1601938.description: Greek mythology character, daughter of Bellerophon

Q161419.label: Oceanus
Q161419.description: ancient Greek god of the earth-encircling river, Oceanos
Q161419.lead: In Greek mythology, Oceanus or Okeanos was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth), and the god of the great river which encircled the entire world. He was the brother and husband of the Titaness Tethys, and by her was the father of the river gods and the Oceanids.

Q161936.label: Death
Q161936.lead: Personifications of death are found in many religions and mythologies. In more modern stories, a character known as the Grim Reaper (usually depicted as a berobed skeleton wielding a scythe) causes the victim's death by coming to collect that person's soul.

Q16332739.label: Pelegon
Q16332739.description: son of Axius in Greek mythology

Q164061.label: Helen of Troy
Q164061.description: daughter of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q164061.lead: Helen, commonly known as Helen of Troy and sometimes as Helen of Sparta, is a figure in Greek mythology said to have been the most beautiful woman in the world. She was believed to have been the daughter of Zeus by Leda or Nemesis, and the sister of Clytemnestra, Castor, Pollux, Philonoe, Phoebe and Timandra.

Q1655397.label: Ialmenus
Q1655397.lead: In Greek mythology, Ialmenus or Ialmenos was a son of Ares and Astyoche, and twin brother of Ascalaphus. Together with his brother he sailed with the Argonauts, among the suitors of Helen, and led the Orchomenian contingent in the Trojan War.

Q167646.label: Paris
Q167646.description: mythological son of Priam, king of Troy
Q167646.lead: Paris, also known as Alexander (Ancient Greek: Ἀλέξανδρος, romanized: Aléxandros), is a figure from Greek mythology who appears in the numerous stories about the Trojan War, including the Iliad. He was prince of Troy, son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba, and younger brother of Prince Hector.

Q1686620.label: Eumelus
Q1686620.description: mythical king of Pherae, son of Admetus

Q170473.label: Priam
Q170473.description: the legendary and last king of Troy during the Trojan war; son of Laomedon
Q170473.lead: In Greek mythology, Priam was the legendary and last king of Troy during the Trojan War. He was the son of Laomedon.

Q170779.label: Cassandra
Q170779.description: mythological prophetess and princess of Troy
Q170779.lead: In Greek mythology, Cassandra, also spelled Kassandra or Casandra, was a Trojan priestess dedicated to the god Apollo and fated by him to utter true prophecies, but never to be believed. Cassandra lived through the Trojan War and survived the sack of the city, but was murdered by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus when Agamemnon brought her to Mycenae as a pallake.

Q171839.label: Menelaus
Q171839.description: mythical king of Sparta, husband of Helen of Troy
Q171839.lead: In Greek mythology, Menelaus was a king of Sparta. According to the Iliad, the Trojan War began as a result of Menelaus' wife, Helen, fleeing to Troy with the Trojan prince Paris.

Q172725.label: Ajax the Great
Q172725.description: son of Telamon in Greek mythology
Q172725.lead: Ajax or Aias is a Greek mythological hero, the son of King Telamon and Periboea, and the half-brother of Teucer.

Q17282472.label: Schedius
Q17282472.description: son of Iphitos and ruler of Phocis

Q17426381.label: Harpalion
Q17426381.description: son of Pylaemenes in Greek mythology

Q1774178.label: Cleopatra
Q1774178.description: Greek mythological person, daughter of Idas and Marpessa
Q1774178.lead: In Greek mythology Cleopatra, sometimes called Alcyone (Ancient Greek: Ἀλκυόνη, romanized: Alkuónē, lit. 'kingfisher') was the daughter of Idas and Marpessa and the wife of Meleager, a Calydonian prince and participant in the Calydonian boar hunt. Together they had a daughter, Polydora.

Q1782641.label: Acamas
Q1782641.lead: In Greek mythology, Acamas or Akamas, was the son of Trojan elder Antenor and Theano. He participated in the Trojan War, and fought on the side of the Trojans.

Q178641.label: Peleus
Q178641.description: son of Aeacus in Greek mythology
Q178641.lead: In Greek mythology, Peleus was a hero, king of Phthia, husband of Thetis and the father of their son Achilles.

Q178831.label: Aurora
Q178831.description: goddess of dawn in Roman mythology
Q178831.lead: In Roman mythology, Aurora is the goddess and personification of the dawn. Aurora is the Latin word for dawn, and she appeared frequently in Latin literature.

Q180237.label: Typhon
Q180237.lead: Typhon, also known as Typhoeus (Τυφωεύς, Typhōeús), Typhaon (Τυφάων, Typháōn) or Typhos (Τυφώς, Typhṓs), was a monstrous serpentine giant and one of the deadliest creatures in Greek mythology. According to Hesiod, Typhon was the son of Gaia and Tartarus.

Q183417.label: Chiron
Q183417.lead: In Greek mythology, Chiron, also Cheiron or Kheiron, was held to be the superlative centaur amongst his brethren since he was called the "wisest and justest of all the centaurs".

Q184216.label: Tethys
Q184216.description: ancient Greek mythological figure; mother of the river gods and the Oceanids
Q184216.lead: In Greek mythology, Tethys was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth), the sister and wife of the Titan Oceanus, and the mother of the river gods and the Oceanids. Although Tethys had no active role in Greek mythology and no established cults, she was depicted in mosaics decorating baths, pools, and triclinia in the Greek East, particularly in Antioch and its suburbs, either alone or with Oceanus.

Q184437.label: Thetis
Q184437.lead: Thetis is a figure from Greek mythology with varying mythological roles. She mainly appears as a sea nymph, a goddess of water, and one of the 50 Nereids, daughters of the ancient sea god Nereus.

Q184570.label: Iris
Q184570.description: the personification of the rainbow in ancient Greek religion and mythology
Q184570.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Iris is a daughter of the gods Thaumas and Electra, and the personification of the rainbow. She functions as a messenger and servant to the Olympians, particularly Hera.

Q186271.label: Patroclus
Q186271.description: son of Menoetius in Greek mythology, a greek hero of the Trojan war
Q186271.lead: Patroclus was a Greek hero of the Trojan War and close companion of the hero Achilles in Greek mythology. Patroclus is an important character in Homer's Iliad.

Q189527.label: Nereus
Q189527.lead: In Greek mythology, Nereus was the eldest son of Pontus (the Sea) and Gaia (the Earth). Nereus and Doris became the parents of 50 daughters (the Nereids) and a son (Nerites), with whom Nereus lived in the Aegean Sea.

Q189872.label: Bellerophon
Q189872.description: Hero in Greek myth who rode Pegasus and killed the Chimera
Q189872.lead: Bellerophon or Bellerophontes or Hipponous (Ancient Greek: Ἱππόνοος, lit. 'horse-knower'), was a divine Corinthian hero of Greek mythology, the son of Poseidon and Eurynome, and the foster son of Glaukos. He was "the greatest hero and slayer of monsters, alongside Cadmus and Perseus, before the days of Heracles".

Q190543.label: Alkmene
Q190543.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcmene or Alcmena ( alk-MEE-nə; Doric Greek: Ἀλκμάνα, romanized: Alkmána; Latin: Alcumena; meaning "strong in wrath") was the wife of Amphitryon, by whom she bore two children, Iphicles and Laonome. She is best known as the mother of Heracles, whose father was the god Zeus.

Q1920680.label: Menoetius
Q1920680.description: son of Actor and father of Patroclus

Q192407.label: Orestes
Q192407.description: son of Agamemnon in Greek mythology
Q192407.lead: In Greek mythology, Orestes or Orestis was the son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, and the brother of Electra and Iphigenia. He was also known by the patronymic Agamemnonides (Ἀγαμεμνονίδης), meaning "son of Agamemnon." He is the subject of multiple Ancient Greek plays (including Aeschylus' Oresteia), which depict his revenge, madness, and purification.

Q192469.label: Atreus
Q192469.description: king of Mycenae, father of Agamemnon
Q192469.lead: In Greek mythology, Atreus was a king of Mycenae in the Peloponnese, the son of Pelops and Hippodamia, and the father of Agamemnon and Menelaus. His descendants became known collectively as the Atreidae (Ancient Greek: Ἀτρείδαι Atreidai).

Q192482.label: Telemachus
Q192482.description: in Greek mythology, the son of Odysseus and Penelope, a character from Homer's "Odyssey"
Q192482.lead: Telemachus is the son of Odysseus and Penelope in Greek mythology, and a central character in Homer's Odyssey. When Telemachus reached manhood, he visited Pylos and Sparta in search of his wandering father.

Q193267.label: Nestor
Q193267.description: wise ruler of Pylos in Greek mythology, son of Neleus
Q193267.lead: In Greek mythology, Nestor of Gerenia was a legendary king of Pylos. He is a prominent secondary character in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, where he appears as an elderly warrior who frequently offers advice to the other characters.

Q193433.label: Hecuba
Q193433.lead: In Greek mythology, Hecuba was the wife of King Priam and queen of Troy during the Trojan War. With Priam, she was the mother of the warriors Hector and Troilus; Helen's suitor Paris; and the prophetess Cassandra.

Q193609.label: Rhadamanthus
Q193609.description: Greek mythology character, son of Zeus and Europa
Q193609.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhadamanthus or Rhadamanthys was a wise king of Crete. As the son of Zeus and Europa he was considered a demigod.

Q19376.label: Andromache
Q19376.description: wife of Hector in Greek mythology
Q19376.lead: In Greek mythology, Andromache was the wife of Hector, daughter of Eetion, and sister to Podes. She was born and raised in the city of Cilician Thebe, over which her father ruled.

Q199923.label: Dione
Q199923.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Dione is an oracular goddess and Titaness. She is primarily known from Book V of Homer's Iliad, where she tends to the wounds suffered by her daughter Aphrodite.

Q20018046.label: Capys
Q20018046.description: son of Assaracus in Greek mythology
Q20018046.lead: In Roman and Greek mythology, Capys was a king of Dardania during the Iliad and Aeneid.

Q206187.label: Aeacus
Q206187.description: son of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q206187.lead: Aeacus was a king of the island of Aegina in Greek mythology. He was a son of Zeus and the nymph Aegina, and the father of the heroes Peleus and Telamon.

Q207663.label: Augeias of Elis
Q207663.description: son of Phorbas in Greek mythology
Q207663.lead: In Greek mythology, Augeas, also called Aegeus, was king of Elis and father of Epicaste. Some ancient authors say that Augeas was one of the Argonauts.

Q208017.label: Acrisius
Q208017.lead: In Greek mythology, Acrisius was a king of Argos. He was the grandfather of the famous Greek demi-god Perseus through his only daughter Danaë.

Q2104755.label: Prothoenor
Q2104755.description: Greek mythical character, Boeotian warrior killed by Polydamas at Troy
Q2104755.lead: In Greek mythology, Prothoenor was one of the Greek leaders in the Trojan War, from Thespiae in Boeotia, son of Areilycus (Archilycus) and Theobule, brother of Arcesilaus; he commanded eight ships. In one account, Prothoenor was the son of Alector and Arteis, and thus a half-brother of Leitus and Clonius.

Q211953.label: Anchises
Q211953.description: father of Aeneas in Greek mythology, lover of Aphrodite
Q211953.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Anchises was a member of the royal family of Troy. He was said to have been the son of King Capys of Dardania and Themiste, daughter of Ilus, who was son of Tros.

Q212087.label: Eurystheus
Q212087.description: king of Mycenae in Greek mythology
Q212087.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurystheus was king of Tiryns, one of three Mycenaean strongholds in the Argolid, although other authors including Homer and Euripides cast him as ruler of Argos.

Q212827.label: Philoctetes
Q212827.lead: Philoctetes, or Philocthetes, according to Greek mythology, was the son of Poeas, king of Meliboea in Thessaly, and Demonassa or Methone. He was a Greek hero, famed as an archer, and a participant in the Trojan War.

Q213621.label: Niobe
Q213621.lead: Niobe was in Greek mythology a daughter of Tantalus and of either Dione or of Eurythemista or Euryanassa. She was the wife of Amphion and the sister of Pelops and Broteas.

Q21548530.label: Amphius
Q21548530.description: king, son of Merops of Percote

Q2300199.label: Meges
Q2300199.lead: In Greek mythology, Mégês Phyleïdês was the commander of Epeans and/or Dulichians during the Trojan War.

Q2305436.label: Othryoneus
Q2305436.lead: Othryoneus is a character in Greek mythology who was the intended husband for Princess Cassandra of Troy during the Trojan War, mentioned in one passage in Homer's Iliad. Othryoneus was from Cabesos, a Homeric site over whose location there has been disagreements since ancient times, some sources suggesting a site in the Troad self and others pointing at the very similar name of the ancient site of Kavissos, today near Feres near Evros.

Q23168.label: Minos
Q23168.description: Greek mythology character, son of Zeus and Europa, king of Crete
Q23168.lead: In Greek mythology, Minos was a king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa. Every nine years, he made King Aegeus pick seven young boys and seven young girls to be sent to Daedalus's creation, the labyrinth, to be eaten by the Minotaur.

Q2317917.label: Helicaon
Q2317917.lead: In Greek mythology, Helicaon or Helikaon was a Trojan warrior and son of the elder Antenor and the priestess Theano. He was the brother of Crino, including Acamas, Agenor, Antheus, Archelochus, Coön, Demoleon, Eurymachus, Glaucus, Hippolochus, Hypsipylus, Iphidamas, Laodamas, Laodocus, Medon, Polybus, and Thersilochus.

Q241070.label: Galatea
Q241070.lead: In Greek mythology, Galatea was the name of the following figures: Galatea, a Nereid who loved the shepherd Acis, and was loved by the cyclops Polyphemus. Galatea, the post-antiquity name given to the statue of a woman created by Pygmalion and brought to life by Aphrodite.

Q244318.label: Briseis
Q244318.description: daughter of Briseus in Greek mythology
Q244318.lead: Briseis, also known as Hippodameia (Ἱπποδάμεια, [hippodámeːa]), is a significant character in the Iliad. Her role as a status symbol is at the heart of the dispute between Achilles and Agamemnon that initiates the plot of Homer's epic.

Q2479077.label: Simoeis
Q2479077.description: god of the Simoeis river, Troad
Q2479077.lead: Simoeis or Simois was a river of the Trojan plain, now called the Dümruk Su (Dümrek Çayı), and the name of its god in Greek mythology.

Q250506.label: Tydeus
Q250506.description: son of Oeneus in Greek mythology
Q250506.lead: Tydeus was an Aetolian hero in Greek mythology, belonging to the generation before the Trojan War. He was one of the Seven against Thebes, and the father of Diomedes, who is frequently known by the patronymic Tydides.

Q254381.label: Peneleus
Q254381.description: son of Hippalcimus in Greek mythology
Q254381.lead: In Greek mythology, Peneleos or, less commonly, Peneleus (Πηνέλεος Pēnéleos), son of Hippalcimus (Hippalmus) and Asterope, was an Achaean soldier in the Trojan War.

Q2547185.label: Agenor
Q2547185.lead: In Greek mythology, Agenor was a Trojan hero.

Q2647181.label: Asius
Q2647181.description: Greek mythical character, King of Arisbe

Q270117.label: Lycurgus of Thrace
Q270117.description: mythological king of the Edoni in Thrace
Q270117.lead: In Greek mythology, Lycurgus was the king of the Edoni in Thrace, son of Dryas, the "oak", and father of a son whose name was also Dryas.

Q2723576.label: Podarge
Q2723576.description: one of the Harpies in Greek mythology
Q2723576.lead: In Greek mythology, Podarge is a harpy, a personification of a swift wind and mate of Zephyrus, the West Wind. She is the mother of Balius and Xanthus — two divine horses renowned for their swiftness and who were gifted to Achilles, running as fast as the wind.

Q27700370.label: Hippocoon
Q27700370.description: Thracian counsellor and kinsman of Rhesus

Q2780953.label: Clonius
Q2780953.description: son of Alector or Alegenor in Greek mythology

Q278930.label: Epeius
Q278930.description: mythical character, Achean soldier who built the Trojan Horse
Q278930.lead: Epeius or Epeus was a mythological Greek soldier during the Trojan War or, in some accounts, one of the Achaean Leaders, at the head of a contingent of 30 ships from the islands of the Cyclades. He was also the architect of the Wooden Horse, by means of which the Achaeans took Troy; he was himself among those warriors who hid inside it.

Q2826489.label: Agathon
Q2826489.description: Greek mythical character, son of Priam
Q2826489.lead: In Greek mythology, Agathon was one of the sons of King Priam of Troy by other women. He was one of the last surviving princes during the Trojan War.

Q29626641.label: Polydorus
Q29626641.description: son of Priam and Laothoe in the Iliad

Q3028709.label: Diomede
Q3028709.description: daughter of Phorbas, captive of Achilles

Q3044434.label: Demoleon
Q3044434.lead: In Greek mythology, Demoleon was a Trojan warrior, son of Antenor and Theano. His father was a counselor to King Priam and his mother was a priestess of Athena.

Q304525.label: Caletor
Q304525.description: Greek mythological character, son of Clytius

Q3084264.label: Hecamede
Q3084264.description: daughter of Arsinous in Greek mythology
Q3084264.lead: In the Iliad, Hecamede, daughter of Arsinoos, was captured from the isle of Tenedos and given as captive to King Nestor. In her most prolonged mention, she serves Kykeon made from Pramnian wine, a medicinal drink, to Nestor and Machaon.

Q3135998.label: Hippolochus
Q3135998.lead: In Greek mythology, Hippolochus was a Lycian prince as the son of King Bellerophon. He was probably the successor of the latter in the kingship of the Lycian land.

Q3136168.label: Hippomachus
Q3136168.description: son of Antimachus in Greek mythology

Q3136176.label: Hippothous
Q3136176.description: mythological Greek character, son of Priam

Q3155123.label: Isander
Q3155123.description: Greek mythical character, son of Bellerophon

Q3155610.label: Isus
Q3155610.lead: In Greek mythology, Isus was a minor character mentioned in Homer's Iliad, one of the 50 sons of King Priam by an unidentified woman. He was killed by Agamemnon.

Q32102.label: Ceres
Q32102.lead: In ancient Roman religion, Ceres was a goddess of agriculture, grain crops, fertility, and motherly relationships. She was originally the central deity in Rome's so-called plebeian or Aventine Triad, then was paired with her daughter Proserpina in what Romans described as "the Greek rites of Ceres".

Q321541.label: Meleager
Q321541.description: son of Oeneus in Greek mythology, king of Calydon
Q321541.lead: Meleager was a hero in Greek mythology, venerated in his temenos at Calydon in Aetolia. He was famed as the host of the Calydonian boar hunt in the epic tradition that was reworked by Homer, and was also mentioned as one of the Argonauts.

Q322639.label: Neoptolemus
Q322639.lead: In Greek mythology, Neoptolemus, originally called Pyrrhus at birth (Πύρρος, Pýrrhos, 'red'), was the son of the mythical warrior Achilles and the princess Deidamia, and the brother of Oneiros. He became the progenitor of the ruling dynasty of the Molossians of ancient Epirus.

Q3266310.label: Polybus
Q3266310.lead: In Greek mythology, Polybus or Polybius was the son of Antenor and Theano. He was the brother of Crino, Acamas, Agenor, Antheus, Archelochus, Coön, Demoleon, Eurymachus, Glaucus, Helicaon, Iphidamas, Laodamas, Laodocus, Medon and Thersilochus.

Q331327.label: Telamon
Q331327.description: one of the Argonauts of Jason, in Greek mythology
Q331327.lead: Telamon in Greek mythology was the son of King Aeacus of Aegina, and Endeïs, a mountain nymph. The elder brother of Peleus, Telamon sailed alongside Jason as one of his Argonauts, and was present at the hunt for the Calydonian Boar.

Q332324.label: Laomedon
Q332324.lead: In Greek mythology, Laomedon was a Trojan king, son of Ilus and thus nephew of Ganymede and Assaracus. Laomedon was variously identified with different parents and siblings, as well as numerous children, including Priam and Tithonus.

Q334787.label: Astyanax
Q334787.lead: In Greek mythology, Astyanax was the son of Hector, the crown prince of Troy, and of his wife, Princess Andromache of Cilician Thebe. His birth name was Scamandrius (in Greek: Σκαμάνδριος Skamandrios, after the river Scamander), but the people of Troy nicknamed him Astyanax (i.e.

Q334817.label: Polynices
Q334817.lead: In Greek mythology, Polynices (also Polyneices) was the son of Oedipus and either Jocasta or Euryganeia, and the brother of Eteocles, Antigone, and Ismene. When Oedipus discovered that he had killed his father and married his mother, he blinded himself and left Thebes, leaving Polynices and Eteocles to rule jointly.

Q3381470.label: Phorcys
Q3381470.description: Phrygian ally of King Priam in the Trojan War
Q3381470.lead: In Greek mythology, Phorcys was a Phrygian ally of King Priam in the Trojan War. Phorcys appears in The Iliad as the leader of the Phrygians, a son of Phaenops.

Q34201.label: Zeus
Q34201.description: Greek god of the sky and king of the gods
Q34201.lead: Zeus is the supreme deity of the Greek pantheon. He is a sky and thunder god in ancient Greek religion and mythology, who rules as king of the gods on Mount Olympus.

Q3473958.label: Satnius
Q3473958.description: son of Enops in Greek mythology

Q35500.label: Aphrodite
Q35500.description: Greek goddess of love, beauty, pleasure, and procreation
Q35500.lead: Aphrodite is an ancient Greek goddess associated with love and beauty. Aphrodite's main cult centers were Cythera, Cyprus, Corinth, and Athens.

Q3559088.label: Podes
Q3559088.description: son of Eetion in Greek mythology, and thus the brother of Andromache, wife of Hector
Q3559088.lead: In Greek mythology, Podes was the son of Eetion, and thus the brother of Andromache, the wife of Hector, whom he is said to have been a feast friend of.

Q3605023.label: Adamas
Q3605023.description: Greek mythical character, son of Asius
Q3605023.lead: In Greek mythology, Adamas was a participant during the Trojan War. He was the son of Asius, son of Hyrtacus, and brother of Phaenops.

Q3606134.label: Aphareus
Q3606134.description: mythical son of Caletor in the Iliad

Q3608994.label: Alcimedon
Q3608994.description: mythological Greek character, son of Laerkes
Q3608994.lead: Alcimedonte or Alcimedon is a character from Greek mythology. He was the son of Laerces and one of the five leaders of the Myrmidons in the contingent led by Achilles during the Trojan War, mentioned by Homer in the Iliad, Books XVI and XVII. When the combat to the death between Patroclus, who was wearing Achilles' armor, and Hector ended with Hector's victory, Alcimedonte took over Achilles' chariot, drawn by the immortal horses Xanthus and Balius, as he was described as an excellent charioteer.

Q3609014.label: Alcmaon
Q3609014.description: son of Thestor in Greek mythology
Q3609014.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcmaon was the son of Thestor. He was one of the Achaean warriors who fought at Troy but was killed by the Lycian leader Sarpedon with a spear.

Q3618410.label: Anthemion
Q3618410.description: Greek mythological character, father of Simoeisius

Q3621497.label: Archeptolemus
Q3621497.description: son of Iphitus in Greek mythology

Q3622225.label: Aretus
Q3622225.description: son of Priam, who tried to steal Achilles' horse

Q3663043.label: Castianeira
Q3663043.description: figure of Greek mythology, a wife of the Trojan king Priam, mother of Gorgythion

Q367819.label: Meriones
Q367819.description: mythical son of Molus of Crete
Q367819.lead: Meriones was the Cretan son of Molus and Melphis or Euippe in Greek mythology. Molus was a half-brother of Idomeneus.

Q3680849.label: Cleitus
Q3680849.description: character in the Iliad, son of Peisenor

Q3702517.label: Dares
Q3702517.description: mythical Greek character, Trojan priest, father of Idaeus and Phegeus

Q3704812.label: Deiochus
Q3704812.description: Achaean soldier killed by Paris during the siege of Troy
Q3704812.lead: This is a list of principal characters in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey.

Q3704816.label: Deipyrus
Q3704816.lead: In Greek mythology, Deïpyrus was an Achaean soldier who participated in the Trojan War. According to one scholiast, some say that he was from Pylos, while others called him a brother to Meriones, a Cretan hero.

Q3705324.label: Democoon
Q3705324.description: son of Priam, who grazes his father's steeds in Abydos
Q3705324.lead: In Greek mythology, Democoon was a Trojan, son of king Priam mentioned in Homer's Iliad, Hyginus's Fabulae and the Bibliotheca. His mother's name is unknown.

Q3712723.label: Dolops
Q3712723.description: mythological Greek character, son of Lampus in the Iliad

Q3718502.label: Echepolus
Q3718502.description: son of Thalysios, Troian, killed by Antilochos

Q3725424.label: Eniopeus
Q3725424.description: charioteer in Homer's Iliad; son of Thebaeus

Q3725538.label: Enops
Q3725538.description: Cattle herder to whom a naiad gave birth to Satnios

Q3726840.label: Epicles
Q3726840.description: Lycian or Trojan prince killed by Ajax

Q3731398.label: Ereuthalion
Q3731398.description: in Greek mythology, giant leader of the Arcadians against the Pylians, slain by Nestor

Q37340.label: Apollo
Q37340.description: god in Greek and later Roman mythology
Q37340.lead: Apollo is one of the Olympian deities in ancient Greek religion and mythology. His numerous functions include light, healing, prophecy, music, poetry, and archery.

Q3791459.label: Iamenus
Q3791459.lead: In Greek mythology, Iamenus was a Trojan hero in the Iliad. Together with Asius, he was slain by Leonteus during the attack of the Trojans on the camp of the Greeks.

Q3792190.label: Iphition
Q3792190.description: son of Otrynteus in Greek mythology

Q3801505.label: Hyperenor
Q3801505.description: son of Panthous in Greek mythology

Q3831220.label: Leucus
Q3831220.description: hero of the Iliad, companion of Odysseus, killed by Antiphus

Q3850790.label: Altes
Q3850790.lead: In Greek mythology, Altes was a Lelegian king who resided at Pedasus, which was situated in or near the Troad. According to Homer's Iliad, Altes was the father of Laothoe, one of the many wives of King Priam.

Q3854654.label: Menesthius
Q3854654.description: son of Spercheus in Greek mythology

Q3854705.label: Menon
Q3854705.lead: In Greek mythology, Menon was a Trojan soldier killed by Leonteus in the Trojan War as detailed by Homer in the Iliad (XII.201).

Q3892897.label: Pammon
Q3892897.description: son of Priam in Greek mythology
Q3892897.lead: In Greek mythology, Pammon was a Trojan prince and one of the sons of King Priam of Troy and Hecuba. He was killed by Achilles' son Neoptolemus during the Trojan War.

Q3905648.label: Peirous
Q3905648.description: son of Imbrasos in Greek mythology
Q3905648.lead: In Greek mythology, Peirous or Peiroos was a Thracian war leader from the city of Aenus and an ally of King Priam during the Trojan War. Peirous was the son of Imbrasus and father of Rhygmus (who fought at Troy alongside his father).

Q3954.label: Neptune
Q3954.description: Roman god of water, particularly the sea, considered equivalent to the Greek Poseidon
Q3954.lead: Neptune is the god of freshwater and the sea in the Roman religion. He is the counterpart of the Greek god Poseidon.

Q3961094.label: Simoeisius
Q3961094.description: son of Anthemion in Greek mythology

Q3973491.label: Stichius
Q3973491.lead: In Greek mythology, Stichius was an Athenian leader who participated in the Trojan War.

Q4002524.label: Ucalegon
Q4002524.lead: Ucalegon was one of the Elders of Troy, whose house was set afire by the Achaeans when they sacked the city. He is one of Priam's friends in the Iliad, and the destruction of his house is referred to in the Aeneid.

Q41410.label: Hades
Q41410.description: god of the underworld in Greek mythology
Q41410.lead: Hades, in the ancient Greek religion and mythology, is the god of the dead and riches and the King of the underworld, with which his name became synonymous. Hades was the eldest son of Cronus and Rhea, although this also made him the last son to be regurgitated by his father.

Q41746.label: Achilles
Q41746.description: Greek mythological hero of the Trojan War
Q41746.lead: In Greek mythology, Achilles or Achilleus (Ancient Greek: Ἀχιλλεύς, romanized: Achilleús) was a hero of the Trojan War who was known as being the greatest of all the Greek warriors. The central character in Homer's Iliad, he was the son of the Nereid Thetis and Peleus, king of Phthia and famous Argonaut.

Q4287919.label: Medon
Q4287919.description: mythological Greek character, son of Oileus

Q440440.label: Althaea
Q440440.lead: In Greek mythology, Althaea, also rendered Althea or Althaia, was queen of Calydon through her marriage to King Oeneus. Althaea appears in myths surrounding the fabled Calydonian boar hunt, and is infamous for murdering her son Meleager.

Q44204.label: Cronus
Q44204.description: ruler of the Titans in Greek mythology
Q44204.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Cronus, Cronos, or Kronos was the leader and youngest of the Titans, the children of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky). Cronus castrated and overthrew his father and then ruled during the mythological Golden Age until he himself was overthrown by his son, Zeus, and imprisoned in Tartarus.

Q44417752.label: Hypsenor
Q44417752.description: son of Dolopion in Greek mythology

Q461212.label: Dardanus
Q461212.description: mythological Greek character, son of Zeus
Q461212.lead: In Greek mythology, Dardanus was the founder of the city of Dardanus at the foot of Mount Ida in the Troad. Dardanus, a son of Zeus and the Pleiad Electra, was a significant figure in Greek mythology.

Q4640.label: Vulcan
Q4640.description: god of both beneficial and hindering fire
Q4640.lead: Vulcan is the god of fire including the fire of volcanoes, deserts, metalworking and the forge in ancient Roman religion and myth. He is often depicted with a blacksmith's hammer.

Q4649.label: Jupiter
Q4649.description: chief deity of Roman state religion
Q4649.lead: In ancient Roman religion and mythology, Jupiter, also known as Jove (nom. and gen.

Q466830.label: Myrmidons
Q466830.lead: In Greek mythology, the Myrmidons or Myrmidones were an ancient Thessalian tribe. In Homer's Iliad, the Myrmidons are the Achaean soldiers commanded by Achilles.

Q467515.label: Zephyrus
Q467515.description: Greek god of the wind from the west, spring, fertility, procreation, luck, rebirth, vegetation, flowers, bees and honey
Q467515.lead: In Greek mythology and religion, Zephyrus, also spelled in English as Zephyr, is the god and personification of the West wind, one of the several wind gods, the Anemoi. The son of Eos (the goddess of the dawn) and Astraeus, Zephyrus is the most gentle and favourable of the winds, associated with flowers, springtime and even procreation.

Q47231.label: Odysseus
Q47231.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Odysseus, also known by the Latin variant Ulysses (UK also ; Latin: Ulysses, Ulixes), is a legendary Greek king of Ithaca and the hero of Homer's epic poem, the Odyssey. Odysseus also plays a key role in Homer's Iliad and other works in that same epic cycle.

Q47652.label: Venus
Q47652.description: Roman goddess of love, sexuality, procreation and pleasure
Q47652.lead: Venus is a Roman goddess whose functions encompass love, beauty, desire, sex, fertility, prosperity, and victory. In Roman mythology, she was the ancestor of the Roman people through her son, Aeneas, who survived the fall of Troy and fled to Italy.

Q4830640.label: Axius
Q4830640.lead: In Greek mythology Axius is a Paeonian river god, the son of Oceanus and Tethys. He was the father of Pelagon, by Periboea, daughter of Acessamenus.

Q502156.label: Pirithous
Q502156.description: son of Ixion in Greek mythology
Q502156.lead: Pirithous, in Greek mythology, was the King of the Lapiths of Larissa in Thessaly, as well as best friend to Theseus.

Q506550.label: Eteocles
Q506550.lead: In Greek mythology, Eteocles was a king of Thebes, the son of Oedipus and either Jocasta or Euryganeia. Oedipus killed his father Laius and married his mother without knowing his relationship to either.

Q508543.label: Aerope
Q508543.description: daughter of Catreus, the king of Crete
Q508543.lead: In Greek mythology, Aerope was a Cretan princess as the daughter of Catreus, king of Crete. She was the sister of Clymene, Apemosyne and Althaemenes.

Q54230.label: Nereids
Q54230.description: sea nymphs in Greek mythology, daughters of Nereus
Q54230.lead: In Greek mythology, the Nereids or Nereides are sea nymphs (female spirits of sea waters), the 50 daughters of the 'Old Man of the Sea' Nereus and the Oceanid Doris, sisters to their brother Nerites.

Q548099.label: Eurynome
Q548099.lead: In Greek mythology Eurynome was an Oceanid and the mother of the Charites by Zeus.

Q570434.label: Idomeneus
Q570434.description: Greek mythical character, King of Crete
Q570434.lead: In Greek mythology, Idomeneus was a Cretan king and commander who led the Cretan armies to the Trojan War, in eighty black ships. He was also one of the suitors of Helen, as well as a comrade of the Telamonian Ajax.

Q571969.label: Antenor
Q571969.lead: In Greek mythology, Antenor was a counselor to King Priam of Troy during the events of the Trojan War.

Q577552.label: Antilochus
Q577552.lead: In Greek mythology, Antilochus was a prince of Pylos and one of the Achaeans in the Trojan War. He was the youngest prince to command troops.

Q582141.label: Antiphus
Q582141.description: son of Priam in Greek mythology

Q599482.label: Tros
Q599482.description: ruler of Troy in Greek mythology
Q599482.lead: In Greek mythology, Tros was the founder of the kingdom of Troy, of which the city of Ilios, founded by his son Ilus took the same name, and the son of Erichthonius by Astyoche (daughter of the river god Simoeis) or of Ilus I, from whom he inherited the throne. Tros was the father of three sons: Ilus, Assaracus and Ganymede and two daughters, Cleopatra and Cleomestra.

Q599489.label: Euphorbus
Q599489.lead: In Greek mythology, Euphorbus was a Trojan hero during the Trojan War.

Q6081853.label: Polites
Q6081853.description: mythological Greek character, Trojan prince, son of Priam
Q6081853.lead: In Greek mythology, Polites was the legitimate son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba, known for his swiftness. He was a brother of 49 other children.

Q611124.label: Chryseis
Q611124.description: mythological Greek character, daughter of Chryses in the Iliad
Q611124.lead: Chryseis is a Trojan woman in Homer's Iliad, the daughter of Chryses. Chryseis, her apparent name in the Iliad, means simply "Chryses' daughter"; later writers give her real name as Astynome (Ἀστυνόμη).

Q637955.label: Neleus
Q637955.description: mythical son of Poseidon or Cretheus and father of Nestor
Q637955.lead: Neleus was a mythological king of Pylos. In some accounts, he was also counted as an Argonaut instead of his son, Nestor.

Q644604.label: Proetus
Q644604.lead: In Greek mythology, Proetus, the son of Abas, was a king of Argos and Tiryns.

Q645312.label: Bacchus
Q645312.lead: In ancient Greek religion and myth, Dionysus is the god of wine-making, orchards, fruit, vegetation, fertility, festivity, insanity, ritual madness, religious ecstasy, and theatre. He was also known as Bacchus (Ancient Greek: Βάκχος Bacchos) by the Greeks (a name later adopted by the Romans) for a frenzy he is said to induce called baccheia.

Q65078400.label: Antiphonus
Q65078400.lead: In Greek mythology, Antiphonus was a Trojan prince as one of the sons of King Priam of Troy.

Q65121579.label: Lycophron
Q65121579.lead: In Greek mythology, Lycophron is a squire of Ajax the Greater during the Trojan War.

Q652220.label: Alcathous
Q652220.description: Greek mythical character, son of Aesyetes

Q655184.label: Cebriones
Q655184.description: son of Priam in Greek mythology
Q655184.lead: In Greek mythology, Cebriones was the illegitimate son of King Priam of Troy and a slave.

Q660196.label: Ascalaphus
Q660196.description: son of Ares in Greek mythology
Q660196.lead: In Greek mythology, Ascalaphus or Askalaphus, was son of Ares and the Minyan princess Astyoche, daughter of King Actor of Orchomenus. Ascalaphus was also a king of the Minyans, and twin brother of Ialmenos.

Q674319.label: Machaon
Q674319.description: character of Greek mythology: son of Asclepius and Coronis, lover of Anticlea; healing hero of the Trojan War; killed by Eurypylus
Q674319.lead: In Greek mythology, Machaon was a son of Asclepius; and the older brother of Podalirius. He and his brother led an army from Tricca in the Trojan War on the side of the Greeks.

Q690613.label: Tlepolemus
Q690613.lead: In Greek mythology, Tlepolemus was the leader of the Rhodian forces in the Trojan War.

Q725527.label: Calchas
Q725527.lead: Calchas is an Argive mantis, or seer, in Greek mythology. Calchas appears in the opening scenes of the Iliad and also has a long literary history after Homer.

Q729332.label: Helenus
Q729332.lead: In Greek mythology, Helenus was a gentle and clever seer. He was also a Trojan prince as the son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba of Troy, and the twin brother of the prophetess Cassandra.

Q736813.label: Deiphobus
Q736813.description: mythical character, son of Priam of Troy
Q736813.lead: In Greek mythology, Deiphobus was a son of Priam and Hecuba. He was a prince of Troy, and the greatest of Priam's sons after Hector.

Q737306.label: Tithonus
Q737306.description: prince of Troy loved by Eos in Greek mythology
Q737306.lead: In Greek mythology, Tithonus was the lover of Eos, Goddess of the Dawn. He was a prince of Troy, the son of King Laomedon by the Naiad Strymo (Στρυμώ).

Q739359.label: Assaracus
Q739359.description: son of Tros in Greek mythology
Q739359.lead: In Greek mythology, Assaracus was a king of Dardania.

Q747657.label: Enyo
Q747657.description: Greek goddess of war and destruction
Q747657.lead: In Greek mythology, Enyo is a war-goddess, frequently associated with the war-god Ares. The Romans identified her with Bellona.

Q748296.label: Laertes
Q748296.lead: In Greek mythology, Laertes was the king of the Cephallenians, an ethnic group who lived both on the Ionian Islands and on the mainland. He presumably inherited the kingdom from his father Arcesius and grandfather Cephalus.

Q748909.label: Asteropaios
Q748909.description: son of Pelegon in Greek mythology
Q748909.lead: In the Iliad, Asteropaios or Asteropaeus was a leader of the Trojan-allied Paeonians along with fellow warrior Pyraechmes.

Q749966.label: Oeneus
Q749966.lead: In Greek mythology, Oeneus was a Calydonian king. He was the first who received a vine-plant from Dionysos.

Q772808.label: Automedon
Q772808.description: son of Diores and charioteer of Achilles
Q772808.lead: In Greek mythology, Automedon, son of Diores, was Achilles' charioteer, who drove the immortal horses Balius and Xanthos. He was from the island of Skyros.

Q776139.label: Semele
Q776139.description: mother of Dionysus in Greek mythology
Q776139.lead: In Greek mythology, Semele, or Thyone (Ancient Greek: Θυώνη, romanized: Thyṓnē), was the youngest daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and the mother of Dionysus by Zeus (her own great-grandfather). Certain elements of the cult of Dionysus and Semele came from the Phrygians.

Q781867.label: Menestheus
Q781867.lead: In Greek mythology, Menestheus was a legendary king of Athens during the Trojan War. He was set up as king by the twins Castor and Pollux when Theseus travelled to the Underworld after abducting their sister, Helen, and exiled Theseus from the city after his return.

Q79999.label: Uranus
Q79999.description: primordial Greek deity, god of the Sky; one of the Greek primordial deities
Q79999.lead: In Greek mythology, Uranus, sometimes written Ouranos (Ancient Greek: Οὐρανός, lit. 'sky', [uːranós]), is the personification of the sky and one of the Greek primordial deities. According to Hesiod, Uranus was the son and husband of Gaia (Earth), with whom he fathered the first generation of Titans.

Q82732.label: Aeneas
Q82732.description: Trojan hero, son of Anchises and Aphrodite
Q82732.lead: Aeneas was a Trojan hero in Greco-Roman mythology, the son of the Trojan prince Anchises and the Greek goddess Aphrodite (equivalent to the Roman Venus). His father was a first cousin of King Priam of Troy (both being great-grandsons of Tros, founder of Troy), making Aeneas a second cousin to Priam's children (such as Hector and Paris).

Q83223.label: Asclepius
Q83223.lead: Asclepius is a hero and god of medicine in ancient Greek religion and mythology. He is the son of Apollo and Coronis, or Arsinoe, or of Apollo alone.

Q849647.label: Briareus
Q849647.lead: In Greek mythology, the Hecatoncheires, also called Hundred-Handers or Centimanes (Latin: Centimani), were three monstrous giants, of enormous size and strength, each with fifty heads and one hundred arms. They were individually named Cottus (the furious), Briareus (or Aegaeon, the sea goat) and Gyges (or Gyes, the long-limbed).

Q852301.label: Chryses
Q852301.description: mythical son of Minos and priest of Apollo
Q852301.lead: In Greek mythology, Chryses was a Trojan priest of Apollo at Chryse, near the city of Troy.

Q854056.label: Dolon
Q854056.description: person in Greek mythology, Trojan soldier
Q854056.lead: In Greek mythology, Dolon fought for Troy during the Trojan War. He volunteered to spy on the Greek camp at the request of Hector, but was captured by Diomedes and Odysseus.

Q858663.label: Electra
Q858663.description: one of the Pleiades in Greek mythology
Q858663.lead: In Greek mythology, Electra was one of the Pleiades, the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione. She lived on the island of Samothrace.

Q871361.label: Protesilaus
Q871361.lead: In Greek mythology, Protesilaus was a hero in the Iliad who was venerated at cult sites in Thessaly and Thrace. Protesilaus was the son of Iphiclus, a "lord of many sheep"; as grandson of the eponymous Phylacos, he was the leader of the Phylaceans.

Q878184.label: Teucer
Q878184.lead: In Greek mythology, Teucer, was the son of King Telamon of Salamis Island and his second wife Hesione, daughter of King Laomedon of Troy. He fought alongside his half-brother, Ajax, in the Trojan War and is the legendary founder of the city of Salamis on Cyprus.

Q917719.label: Sarpedon
Q917719.description: Greek mythology character, son of Zeus and Europa

Q9250189.label: Echius
Q9250189.description: figure of Greek mythology, Greek, father of Mekisteus, killed by Polites

Q93172.label: Gaia
Q93172.description: Greek primordial deity, the personification of the Earth
Q93172.lead: In Greek mythology, Gaia, also spelled Gaea, is the personification of Earth. She is the mother of Uranus (Sky), with whom she conceived the Titans (themselves parents of many of the Olympian gods), the Cyclopes, and the Giants, as well as of Pontus (Sea), from whose union she bore the primordial sea gods.

Q932325.label: Marpessa
Q932325.lead: In Greek mythology, Marpessa was an Aetolian princess and a granddaughter of Ares.

Q956906.label: Thrasymedes
Q956906.lead: In Greek mythology, Thrasymedes was a prince of Pylos and a participant in the Trojan War.

Q99463251.label: Pisander
Q99463251.description: character in the Iliad, killed by Menelaus
